blocks.html: A long word can look like a wall of letters. Look again and you will often find it is built from parts, like train cars hooked together. Take unbreakable: un- (not) + break + -able (able to be). Put the parts together and the meaning falls out: “not able to be broken.”

Many roots are not English words on their own. cred (believe) and spect (look) came from Latin, so you meet them only inside words: credible, incredulous, inspect, spectator. Once you know a root, every word built on it gets easier. Here is one root, port (carry), with its family:

steps: Find the prefix at the front: trans-, which means “across.”
Find the suffix at the end: -able, which means “able to be.”

blocks.html: Splitting a word by its letters alone. The pen in repent is not a writing pen, and uncle does not start with un-: these letters only look like parts. A part is a clue, not a guarantee. Use it to make a guess, then check the guess against the sentence the word is in.

A good habit for any new word: (1) look for a prefix, (2) look for a suffix, (3) see what root is left, (4) put the meanings together, and (5) test your guess in the sentence. The rest of this course teaches the parts that show up most often in strong writing.

blocks.html: English borrowed a huge number of words from Latin, the language of ancient Rome. Many came through French, which grew out of Latin. English also borrowed from ancient Greek, especially for ideas, science and learning. So two parts can mean the same thing: Latin uni- and Greek mono- both mean “one” (a unicycle and a monorail each have one of something).

blocks.html: Clues that a part is Greek: ph said like f (philanthropist), ch said like k (chronic), y used as a vowel (synchronize, polymath) and th (pathos, hypothesis). Latin parts make up most everyday long words: credible, conspicuous, intermittent.

Knowing which language a part comes from helps in two ways. First, it tells you which partner part to expect: Greek parts tend to join other Greek parts (philanthropist is all Greek). Second, it helps with look-alike parts: Greek a- means “without” in apathy, but the a- in English asleep means “on.”

blocks.html: Treating every root as Latin. The clues ph, ch said like k, y and th point to Greek (philanthropist, chronic, synchronize, pathos). And some words mix the two languages: television joins Greek tele (far) to Latin vision (seeing), and automobile joins Greek auto (self) to Latin mobile (moving).
Spelling clues are hints, not rules. Phone and photo are Greek, but a word like shepherd has a p-h made of two separate sounds and is plain English. Use the clue together with the meaning.

blocks.html: The quickest way to flip a word into its opposite is to put “not” in front. English has three prefixes for that. un- is the old English one (unkind, unhappy). in- came with Latin words (invisible, incredible). non- is plain and blunt (nonstop, nonfiction).

blocks.html: Reading every in- as “not.” A different prefix in- means “in” or “into”: inhale (breathe in), incite (stir into action), inundate (flood into). The trickiest case is inflammable: it means easily set on fire, the same as flammable, because its in- means “into” (into flame). Signs say flammable for exactly this reason.
To tell the two in-s apart, try “not”: incredible = not believable works, so its in- means not. Inhale = “not hale” makes no sense, so its in- means into.

A word with a story: an anecdote is a short personal story. The Greek word meant “things not given out,” that is, unpublished tales. That is why anecdotal evidence means evidence from personal stories rather than careful study.

blocks.html: Two small Latin parts sort a whole family of words into good and bad. bene- means “well” (you know it from benefit) and mal- means “badly” (you know it from malfunction: something that works badly). Put one in front of the same root and the meaning flips.

blocks.html: bene- = well, good. mal- (also male-) = badly, bad. A bene- word points to kindness or help; a mal- word points to harm, illness or trouble.

The clearest pair is benevolent and malevolent. Both end in vol (wish, will, as in volunteer). A benevolent person wishes others well; a malevolent one wishes them harm. Watch for the same trick in other pairs: benefactor (one who does good) and malefactor (one who does wrong).

blocks.html: Greek had its own pair for good and bad. eu- means “good” or “well,” and dys- means “bad” or “difficult.” You may know dysfunction (working badly). These parts are fewer than bene- and mal-, but the words they build show up often in reading.

A eulogy is “good words” (eu- + log, word), a speech of praise. Euphoric comes from a Greek word for “bearing well”: so happy you feel you could carry anything.

blocks.html: Mixing up eulogy and elegy. A eulogy (eu-, good) is a speech of praise, often given at a funeral. An elegy is a sad poem; it has no eu-. And eu- is a clue only at the start of a word: the e-u inside feud or neutral is not this part.

A word pair to know: a dystopia (dys-, bad + top, place) is an imagined society where life is miserable. Its opposite is a utopia, an imagined perfect society. That name was made from Greek words meaning “no place,” a hint that such a perfect place may not exist.

entry.etym: From Latin transire, “to go across, to pass by”: trans (across) + ire (to go).

blocks.html: Reading every per- as “through” a place. In many words it just means “thoroughly” and makes the word stronger: to perturb is to disturb thoroughly, not to disturb through something. And per- is not pre- (before): perspective and prescient start with different prefixes.
Both transient and transitory come from a Latin verb meaning “to go across” (trans- + ire, to go). A transient visitor is passing through; a transitory feeling passes quickly.

blocks.html: The largest ocean on Earth is the Pacific, whose name means “peaceful.” pac (also pax) means “peace.” A close neighbor, plac, means “please” or “calm”: a placid lake is calm. And the opposite of peace, bell, means “war”: a rebel wages war again.

entry.def: a comparison that explains one thing by its likeness to another
entry.ex: The coach used an {analogy}: a team is like a clock, and every little gear matters.
entry.ctx: To explain how the computer’s memory works, the author drew an {analogy} to a library, with files as books and the processor as a busy librarian.
entry.etym: From Greek analogia, “proportion”: ana (according to) + logos (ratio, reason).

mn.text: To explain how the brain stores memories, Professor Edwin points from his head to his laptop: “It works like this!” That comparison is an {analogy}.

blocks.html: Reading every log as “study of.” -logy at the end of a word usually means the study of (biology), but log elsewhere often means word or speech: a eulogy is not “the study of good”; it is a speech of praise.

blocks.html: Greek gave English its words for who is in charge. -cracy (also -crat) means “rule” or “power”: democracy is rule by the people (dem, people). -archy (also -arch) means “rule” or “chief”: a monarchy is ruled by one (mon, one). And auto- means “self”: an automatic door opens by itself.

blocks.html: -cracy, -crat = rule, power. -archy, -arch = rule, chief, first. auto- = self.

Put a word for “who” in front and you name a kind of rule. autocrat: a self-ruler, one person with total power. oligarchy: rule by a few (olig, few). anarchy: no ruler at all (an-, without). bureaucracy: rule by offices (bureau, French for desk or office).

blocks.title: Use the parts
blocks.q: In the old city, a handful of rich families made every decision. Was it a democracy, a monarchy or an oligarchy?
steps: democracy: demo (people) + -cracy: rule by the people. Not this one.
monarchy: mon (one) + -archy: rule by one. Not this one either.
oligarchy: olig (few) + -archy: rule by a few. A handful of families is a few.
blocks.a: An oligarchy.

entry.def: a ruler who holds total power alone
entry.ex: The old czar was an {autocrat} who answered to no parliament.
entry.ctx: The club’s founder ran it like an {autocrat}, making every decision himself and never once asking the members to vote.
entry.etym: From Greek autokrates, “ruling by oneself”: autos (self) + kratos (power).

mn.text: King Victor signs every order himself and waves away his advisers: “I decide!” A ruler who holds all the power alone is an {autocrat}.

entry.def: a system that ranks people or things one above another
entry.ex: In the army’s {hierarchy}, a general outranks a colonel, and a colonel outranks a captain.
entry.ctx: The kitchen ran on a strict {hierarchy}: the head chef gave orders to the cooks, the cooks to the helpers, and the helpers to the new dishwasher.
entry.etym: From Greek hierarkhia, “rule of a high priest”: hieros (sacred) + arkhein (to rule); later, any ranking from top to bottom.

mn.text: At the castle the king stands highest, then the knight, then the cook. That ranking from higher to lower is a {hierarchy}.

blocks.html: arch does not always mean rule. It can also mean “chief” or “first”: an archenemy is a chief enemy, and an archetype is a first model that others copy. And a hierarchy is now any ranking from top to bottom, not just one run by priests.

blocks.html: To generate electricity is to produce it, a gene passes traits from parents to children and a genre is a kind of story. All three come from gen, a root that Greek and Latin share, meaning “birth,” “kind” or “produce.” A second Greek root, morph, means “form” or “shape”: a caterpillar’s metamorphosis is its change of shape.

blocks.title: Two look-alikes
blocks.q: Which word fits: (1) “Lila’s ______ plan used a garden hose to water every plant at once.” (2) “The ______ toddler believed every word of the story.”
steps: Both words have in- + gen, the root of birth.
ingenious: full of inborn talent, so clever and inventive.
ingenuous: as innocent as someone newly born, so trusting and frank.
blocks.a: (1) ingenious; (2) ingenuous.

entry.def: very clever and inventive
entry.ex: Sami rigged an {ingenious} pulley that lowers snacks down to his bottom bunk.
entry.ctx: The flood had washed out the footbridge, but the villagers came up with an {ingenious} fix: they lashed empty barrels together into a floating walkway.
entry.etym: From Latin ingeniosus, from ingenium, “natural talent, cleverness,” the same source as engine and engineer.

mn.text: Dev’s robot sorts the laundry by color and folds every sock: an idea worthy of a genius. It is {ingenious}.

entry.def: giving human form or traits to animals or things
entry.ex: Fairy tales are full of {anthropomorphic} animals who talk and wear clothes.
entry.ctx: The cartoon gave the toaster {anthropomorphic} features, a smiling face and waving arms, so that it seemed like a cheerful friend.
entry.etym: From Greek anthropomorphos, “shaped like a human”: anthropos (human being) + morphe (form).

mn.text: In Lila’s picture book, the cat sits at the breakfast table, sips tea and says “Good morning!” just like a person: the cat is {anthropomorphic}.

blocks.html: gen appears in words so different you may miss it: genesis, ingenious, ingenuous, engender and genial (friendly and cheerful) all trace back to it. And do not confuse ingenious (clever) with ingenuous (innocent).

blocks.html: A suffix at the end of a word often tells you what kind of word it is. These four endings make adjectives, words that describe: famous, active, readable, heroic.

blocks.html: -ous (also -ious, -uous) = full of, having. -ive = tending to, doing. -ible, -able = able to be, worth being. -ic, -ical = having to do with, like.

The ending tells you the word’s job; the root tells you its meaning. Put them together: timorous is timor (fear) + -ous (full of), full of fear. malleable is malle (hammer) + -able: able to be hammered into shape. cryptic is crypt (hidden) + -ic: having to do with hidden things.

entry.def: easily shaped or bent; also, easily influenced
entry.ex: Warm wax is {malleable}, so the children pressed it into star shapes.
entry.ctx: Young children’s tastes are {malleable}; a toddler who hates peas this month may ask for seconds next month after seeing an older cousin enjoy them.

blocks.html: Expecting the ending to tell you the meaning. It tells you the part of speech, not what the word means: copious (plentiful), pernicious (harmful) and impetuous (rash) are all adjectives in -ous, but they mean very different things. Use the root for the meaning.

blocks.html: These endings make nouns, words that name a thing, a quality or a person. Add -ity to able and you get ability. Add -tion to act and you get action. Add -ist to art and you get artist, a person who makes art.

blocks.html: -ity, -ty = the quality of being. -tion, -sion = the act or result of. -ance, -ence, -ancy, -ency = the state or act of. -ism = a belief or practice; -ist = a person who.

Many list words are nouns made from adjectives or verbs you may know. brevity is the quality of being brief. veracity is the quality of being truthful (ver, true). cessation is the act of ceasing. credence is the state of believing. A hedonist is a person who lives for pleasure (hedon, pleasure).

blocks.title: Noun or adjective?
blocks.q: Which word fits: “No one doubted the ______ of her story.” Choices: veracious, veracity.
steps: After the and before of, the sentence needs a noun.
-ity makes nouns: veracity, “truthfulness.”
veracious (with -ous) is the adjective, “truthful.”

entry.def: shortness, especially in speech or writing
entry.ex: The {brevity} of the speech delighted the hungry dinner guests.
entry.ctx: Teachers praised her essay for its {brevity}: where others wrote ten pages, she made the same points clearly in three.
entry.etym: From Latin brevitas, from brevis, “short,” the same root as brief and abbreviate.

mn.text: Nobody calls little Theodore by his whole name; he is just Theo. Brev- means brief, and {brevity} is the art of keeping it short.

blocks.html: Using the adjective where a noun belongs, or the other way around. veracity (noun, truthfulness) is not veracious (adjective, truthful); credence (noun) is not credible (adjective). The ending decides how the word fits the sentence.

blocks.html: These endings make verbs, words for doing. Add -ate to active and you get activate; add -ify to simple and you get simplify; add -ize to modern and you get modernize. All three mean, roughly, “to make” or “to cause.”

blocks.html: -ate = to make, to act on. -ify, -fy = to make, to become. -ize = to make, to treat as.

Read the root, then add “to make.” verify: to make (show) true (ver). pacify: to make peaceful (pac). rectify: to make right (rect, right, as in rectangle). nullify: to make nothing (null). alleviate: to make light. synchronize: to make happen at the same time.

blocks.title: One spelling, two words
blocks.q: Say each advocate aloud: (1) “I advocate a longer recess.” (2) “She is an advocate for the park.” How are they different?
steps: In (1), advocate is a verb, and the -ate is said “ayt”: AD-vuh-kayt.
In (2), it is a noun, and the -ate is said “it”: AD-vuh-kit.
The same pattern holds for separate, estimate and duplicate.
blocks.a: The verb ends in “ayt”; the noun ends in “it.”

entry.def: to make pain or trouble easier to bear
entry.ex: An extra checkout lane helped {alleviate} the long lines at the store.
entry.ctx: The volunteers could not end the drought, but they could {alleviate} its effects: they trucked in fresh water and shared it with every farm in the valley.
entry.etym: From Latin alleviare, “to lighten”: ad (to) + levis (light).

mn.text: Kai staggers under a heavy crate until Sven lifts it onto his own broad shoulders. Taking some of the weight is a way to {alleviate} a burden.

blocks.html: Assuming every word that ends in -ate is a verb. Considerate and obstinate are adjectives, and in them the ending is said “it,” not “ayt.” Check how the word is used in the sentence before you decide.
